title: Gases
subject: Chemistry

kit.name: Limewater (In 2 separate test tubes with a straw)

method:
1. Follow the method below to prepare and test for oxygen gas:

a) Put about 5 cm³ of hydrogen peroxide into a boiling tube.

b) Add 1 small spatula of manganese(IV) dioxide.

c) Hold the boiling tube with test-tube holders at a 45° angle.

d) Light a splint and allow it to burn for a few seconds.
1. e) Blow out the flame so that the end remains glowing.

c) Add a few marble chips to the acid.
1. d) Immediately attach a delivery tube and place the far end of the delivery tube into the limewater.

title: Paper chromatography of ink

kit.name: Adhesive tape (clear) (Small amount; To attach paper to glass rod)

Ink (water-soluble felt tip pen ink) (sample; Different colours: black, red, blue, green, etc.)
Alternative: Water-soluble dyes (sample; Food colouring or commercial dyes)

method:
1. Draw with a pencil a baseline at the bottom of the chromatography paper (approximately 1.5 cm high).
2. Place a drop of the ink or dye on this baseline.
3. Place approximately 20 cm³ of water into a beaker.
4. Attach the chromatography paper to the glass rod using adhesive tape, suspending it vertically.
5. Place the chromatogram inside the beaker so the baseline is just above the water level (solvent should not wash the dye away).
6. Observe the solvent (water) moving up the chromatography paper, separating the ink mixture into coloured bands.
7. When the solvent has travelled approximately three-quarters of the way up the paper, remove the chromatogram.
8. Immediately mark the solvent front with a pencil (water quickly evaporates).
9. Measure the distance travelled by the solvent and the distance travelled by each coloured spot from the baseline.
10. Calculate Rf values for each spot using: Rf = distance travelled by substance
11. distance travelled by solvent.

method:

4. Filter the mixture into a conical flask.

title: Solubility
subject: Chemistry
method:
Task A – stirring vs no stirring
1. Measure 100 cm³ of distilled water into a beaker.
2. Place a sugar cube in the water WITHOUT stirring.
3. Time how long the cube takes to dissolve completely.
4. Repeat with another cube, stirring continuously.
5. Compare the dissolving times (stirred vs not stirred).

Task B – granulated vs powder
1. Measure 100 cm³ of distilled water into a beaker.
2. Weigh 2 g of granulated sugar and add it to the water.
3. Stir and record the time to dissolve completely.
4. Repeat with 2 g of powdered sugar.
5. Record all results in a table with headings and units.

Task C – high vs low temperature
1. Heat water to three temperatures (e.g. 20 °C, 40 °C, 60 °C).
2. Measure 100 cm³ of water at each temperature with the measuring cylinder.
3. Add 2 g of granulated sugar to each and stir.
4. Record the dissolving time at each temperature.
5. Make a results table of temperature against dissolving time and identify any anomalous results.

risks.hazard: Hot water can scald – handle it carefully and let beakers cool before handling.
risks.control:
Use heat-resistant gloves for hot equipment.
Make sure water baths are stable and cannot tip over.
Do not leave Bunsen burners unattended.
Wear eye protection when heating water.

method:
1. Set up the apparatus as shown in the diagram
2. In the middle of the paper use a ruler to mark a straight line about 10 cm long

4. Place the mirror on the first line as shown in the diagram above
5. Switch on the ray box and aim a beam of light at the point where the two drawn lines cross at an angle

Use the pencil to mark two positions of the light beam:
1. A point just after leaving the ray box
2. The point on the reflected beam about 10 cm away from the mirror
3. Remove the ray box and mirror

5. Use the protractor to measure the two angles from the 90° line. The angle for the ray towards the mirror is the angle of incidence, and the other is the angle of reflection

title: Reactions of metals

kit.name: Small piece of magnesium ribbon (1–2 cm)

Magnesium oxide (Copper(II) oxide will also work)

method:
Station 1 – Hydrogen Gas Test (Acid + Magnesium)
1. Add 2–3 cm of dilute HCl to the test tube.
2. Drop in the magnesium.
3. As soon as bubbles appear, light a splint.
4. Hold the lit splint at the mouth of the tube.
5. A squeaky pop = hydrogen present.

Station 2 – Carbon Dioxide Gas Test (Acid + Carbonate + Limewater)
1. Half-fill one test tube with limewater.
2. Put a small spatula of marble chips in the second tube.
3. Add 2–3 cm of dilute HCl to the marble chips and quickly fit the bung.
4. Put the end of the delivery tube into the limewater.

Observe:
1. Limewater turns cloudy/milky → carbon dioxide present (positive test).
2. Limewater stays clear → gas is not CO₂ (negative test).

Station 3 – Metal Oxide + Acid (Neutralisation and pH)
1. Add 2–3 cm of dilute acid to a test tube.
2. Add 1–2 small spatulas of metal oxide and swirl.
3. When reaction slows, take a few drops of the mixture.
4. Add universal indicator (or dip indicator paper).
5. Compare to pH chart; record pH.
6. Write: metal oxide + acid → metal salt + water.

Station 4 – Filtration: Separating an Insoluble Solid

LAB TECH PREP before lesson:
1. Make a warm blue mixture by reacting copper oxide with dilute sulfuric acid until some black solid is left (acid neutralised, CuO in excess).
2. Put a small beaker of this “reaction mixture” at the station for each group.
3. Fold and place filter paper in the funnel.
4. Put the funnel into the conical flask.
5. Carefully pour the mixture into the funnel using a glass rod to guide the liquid.

Watch:
1. Residue (black solid) stays on the filter paper.
2. Filtrate (blue solution) collects in the flask.
3. Record which part you would keep if you wanted pure copper sulfate solution (the filtrate).

Station 5 – Crystallisation: Copper Sulfate from Solution

LAB TECH PREP before lesson:
1. Provide each group with a beaker of clear copper sulfate solution (no solid).
2. This can be the filtrate you prepared separately, but it must be ready at the station so any group can start here.
3. Pour some copper sulfate solution into the evaporating basin.
4. Place the basin on the gauze over a tripod and heat gently.
5. Allow some water to evaporate until the solution looks more concentrated (deeper blue, small crust at edge).
6. Turn off the heat and leave the basin to cool.
7. As it cools, copper sulfate crystals will form (or compare with a dish of pre-made crystals).
8. Suggested concentrations by station

Station 1 – H₂ test (Mg + HCl)
1. Dilute hydrochloric acid: 0.5 mol/dm³
2. (If you only have 1.0 M in the prep room, dilute 1:1 with water.)

Station 2 – CO₂ test (carbonate + acid + limewater)
1. Dilute hydrochloric (or sulfuric) acid: 0.5 mol/dm³
2. Limewater: standard lab limewater (saturated Ca(OH)₂, usually around 0.02 mol/dm³; just use “limewater” for students).

Station 3 – Metal oxide + acid (neutralisation + pH)
1. Same acid as above: 0.5 mol/dm³ HCl or 0.5 mol/dm³ H₂SO₄

Station 4 – Filtration (copper oxide + copper sulfate solution mixture)
1. Start with 0.5 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid to make the mixture.
2. The resulting copper sulfate solution will be ≈ 0.5 mol/dm³ CuSO₄ before any extra dilution.

Station 5 – Crystallisation (copper sulfate solution)
1. Use 0.5 mol/dm³ CuSO₄ solution, or dilute to 0.25 mol/dm³ if you want slower, gentler crystal growth.

title: Food tests

kit.name: Water bath (Already set at 60oC with Test tube racks in them)

method:
1. Place 5 cm3 of sample solution to be tested in a test tube.
2. Add several drops of Benedict’s solution into the test tube.
3. Place the test tube in a beaker of boiling water for 5 minutes.
4. Observe the colour of the solution in the test tube. If the blue Benedict’s has changed colour from light blue to orange/red then there is GLUCOSE present.
5. Place 5 cm3 of sample solution to be tested in a test tube.
6. Add several drops of Iodine solution into the test tube.
7. Observe the colour of the solution in the test tube. If iodine turns from orange/brown to black then STARCH is present.
8. Place 5 cm3 of sample solution to be tested in a test tube.
9. Add several drops of Biuret reagent into the test tube.
10. Observe the colour of the solution in the test tube. If the solution turns from light blue to purple then PROTEIN is present.
11. Emulsion Test
12. Grind up the food to be tested with a dry pestle and mortar.
13. Add 2 cm3 of the sample solution to a test tube
14. Add 5 cm3 of absolute ethanol to the same test tube.
15. Stopper the test tube with a bung and shake it well.
16. Leave the test tube in a test tube rack until the particles have settled. This allows the lipids to dissolve in the ethanol.
17. Strain the ethanol solution off into another test tube (leave the food debris behind).
18. Add 3 cm3 of cold water to the ethanol solution. If the solution turns from clear to milky (cloudy white) then LIPIDS are present.
19. Grease Spot Test
20. Rub a dry, solid piece of food against a piece of filter paper (test sample).
21. To the same paper, add a drop of cooking oil (positive control) and a drop of water (negative control).
22. Circle the spots with a pencil.
23. Hold the filter paper up against a lamp and register what you observe.
24. After 10 minutes examine it again. If the spot from the food sample did not disappear then LIPIDS are present.

1. Set up the apparatus as shown in EXAMPLE.

3. Fix the rubber bungs in the mouth of the boiling tubes. In each boiling tube, the end of one delivery tube should dip in the limewater/ hydrogen carbonate indicator, but the end of the other delivery tube should not.

title: Preparation of copper sulfate crystals
subject: Chemistry
method:
1. Use a measuring cylinder to add 20 mL of sulfuric acid in a test tube
2. Gently heat the beaker of water on a Bunsen flame and place the test tube inside of the water for a couple of minutes. Care needs to be taken not to get the acid too hot and certainly not to boiling point. The dilute sulfuric acid needs to be warmed because the reaction with copper (II) oxide is very slow at room temperature.
3. When the acid is hot enough (just before it starts to boil), turn off the burner. 4. Use a spatula to add small portions of copper (II) oxide to the acid. Stir the mixture gently with a glass rod for up to half a minute after each addition. Continue to do this if, after stirring, the black powder disappears, and the solution is clear blue. Stop adding it when some black powder remains after stirring (excess).
5. Allow the solution to cool slightly while you set up the funnel in the conical flask. Fold the filter paper to fit the filter funnel and put it in the funnel.
6. Gently swirl the contents of the beaker to mix and then filter the warm mixture into the conical flask to remove the excess copper oxide.
7. Allow to filter through. A clear blue solution of copper (II) sulfate should collect in the flask. If the solution is not clear, and black powder remains in it, you will need to repeat the filtration. 8. Pour the filtrate into an evaporating basin.
9. Warm the evaporating basin gently by placing it on top of a water beaker in the Bunsen burner (water bath).
10. Evaporate the contents of the basin until you see blue crystals appearing around the edge of the solution. Take care not to allow the solution to boil dry. If you see any fumes, switch off the burner at once.
11. Put the basin and solution aside to cool and crystallise.
12. When cold, filter the solution and allow the pure blue crystals of copper (II) sulfate to dry in a low temperature oven or the air (you can place them in a watch glass). Leaving the filtrate for the water to fully evaporate is not suitable, since any water-soluble impurities in the original copper (II) oxide will also crystallize and contaminate the copper(II) sulfate.

title: Electrostatic charging
subject: Physics
method:
1. When insulating materials rub against each other, they may become electrically charged. Electrons, which are negatively charged, may be ‘rubbed off’ one material and on to the other. The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged. The material that loses electrons is left with a positive charge. A gold leaf electroscope can be used to investigate the nature of the charge on an object. One type of charged object will make the foil lift up and the other will make the foil drop back down again.
2. Charge your electroscope using a high voltage supply (the electroscope can be charged safely using an approved 5 kV laboratory power supply). Note whether your electroscope is positively or negatively charged.
3. Rub an insulator with a duster and hold the insulator close to the electroscope. When a polythene rod is rubbed with a duster, the friction causes electrons to gain energy. Electrons gain enough energy to leave the atom and ‘rub off’ onto the polythene rod. The polythene rod has gained electrons, giving it a negative charge. The duster has lost electrons, giving it a positive charge.
4. From the movement of the electroscope leaf, deduce whether: a) the insulator is charged; b) the sign of the charge.
5. Record our results, noting the duster, the insulator and the sign of the charge on the duster and on the insulator.
6. Repeat the proceed for other pairs of insulators and dusters.

method:
1. Investigating the specific heat capacity of materials including water and some solids
2. The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius. To calculate the change in thermal energy in a substance we use the equation: change in thermal energy (ΔQ) = mass (m) × specific heat capacity (c) × temperature change (ΔT). Using a 30 W heater for 10 minutes provides 10 × 60 × 30 = 18 000 J. This would be sufficient to raise the temperature of 1 kg of copper from room temperature to about 70 °C, aluminium to about 40 °C and iron to 55 °C. This supports the idea that 10 minutes is an adequate length of time for the experiment.

title: Membrane permeability in beetroot
subject: Biology

kit.name: Water bath with clean water at 80°C

method:
1. Preparation of washed beetroot cylinders
2. First prepare 10 cylinders of beetroot.
3. Cut them out of the beetroot with a "cork borer". Using a knife, ruler and white tile, trim them all to the same length. Aim for 2 cm length, but you might have to use shorter pieces.
4. Wash the cylinders thoroughly with water until the water runs clear and pat dry gently with a paper towel.
5. The key thing is that they are all the same length.
6. Prepare 10 diffusion solutions – where the beetroot will rest after heating
7. Set up 10 test tubes into 2 test tube racks.
8. Put 5 mL of distilled water into each test tube.
9. Put each rack onto a piece of A4 paper for noting stopwatch times later.
10. Label the tubes in the rack with the temperature of the Heat Treatment the beetroot will have received before diffusion. “70°C”, “65°C”, “60°C”, etc. to 25°C.
11. Note: these solutions will be a room temperature.
12. Heat Treatment
13. This procedure requires good preparation as the temperature cools quickly at the beginning.
14. Set up a clean electronic water bath at 80°C.
15. Use water from the electronic water bath to make a "beaker water bath" using 150 mL of hot water at 80°C in a 250 mLbeaker. Put a thermometer in it too.
16. When the water has cooled to 70°C put in the first beetroot cylinder, for exactly 60 seconds.
17. Leave the stopwatch running for the whole experiment.
18. Take out the beetroot and put it into the diffusion solution labelled 70°C for 15 minutes. (Note the time on the stopwatch on the A4 paper – you will leave it for 15 minutes).
19. When your water bath has cooled to 65°C put in the next beetroot cylinder, for 60 seconds.
20. Put this beetroot cylinder into the diffusion solution labelled 70°C for 15 minutes.
21. Repeat steps 5 & 6 again at 60°C, 55°C, 50°C and so on to 25°C.
22. Ensure that all the beetroot samples have exactly
23. 60 seconds heat treatment and
24. 15 minutes diffusion time to make this a fair test.
25. Take each piece of beetroot out of the diffusion solutions after exactly 15 minutes.
26. Save the labelled diffusion solutions for the colorimeter.
27. Record notes for your qualitative observations.
28. Colorimeter Readings
29. When more pigment has diffused out of the beetroot cells the diffusion solution will be a darker purple colour. We can measure the colour intensity using a colorimeter.
30. Two thirds fill the plastic colorimeter cuvette with the diffusion solution.
31. Set the colorimeter to a blue/ green filter (or wavelength of 530 nm) and to measure transmission
32. Zero the colorimeter using a blank cuvette filled with distilled water.
33. Put the cuvette with the diffusion solution into the colorimeter slot. Check the mark on the cuvette is at the front.
34. Note down the reading which you get.
35. Check that you are measuring the amount of light absorbed by the beetroot pigment. (Measuring the amount of light passing through your solution, % Transmission)
36. Repeat with all the other solutions and record your results in a table of your own.
37. Note the uncertainty, i.e. the precision of your colorimeter.

RESULTS AND CONCLUSION
1. Present your colorimeter readings for each heat treatment in a clear table of raw data.
2. (Optional) Plot a graph of mean percentage transmission against temperature.
3. Include the uncertainties for each measurement.
4. Include your qualitative observations.
5. Process your experiment results to show the effect of the heat treatment on the diffusion of the purple pigment. Identify the thermal death point (the point when integral proteins in the membrane denature), if you can.
6. Write a conclusion which refers to the aims of the experiment, explains what you have found out, and includes some of the biology behind it.
7. Find something in a text book which either supports or disagrees with your conclusion.
8. Evaluate the limitations of the experiment and your data and suggest specific ways to improve the experiment.

4. Attach the chromatography paper to the cork. Adjust the length of the paper so that when it is inserted into the test tube, it will touch the bottom without curling.
5. Place plant material in a mortar, (add a pinch of sand – optional) and grind with the pestle.

10. Carefully lower the chromatography paper, into the vial/test tube so that the paper dips into the solvent but the pigment spot is above the surface of the solvent.
11. Leave the chromatogram to develop. When the solvent front is close to the top remove the chromatogram and place it on a white tile. Close the vial to minimise evaporation of the running solvent.
12. Immediately mark the location of the solvent front using a pencil before the solvent evaporates.
13. Photograph the chromatogram and mark the location of each coloured spot.

title: DNA extraction

method:
1. Begin by peeling the kiwi fruit and cutting it into small pieces.
2. Place the kiwi pieces into a Ziploc bag and mash them with your hands or a spoon.
3. Add 2-3 teaspoons of liquid dish soap to the bag, seal it, and gently mix the contents by massaging the bag.
4. Add 1/4 teaspoon of table salt to the bag, reseal it, and mix the contents by gently inverting the bag several times.
5. Let the mixture sit for 5-10 minutes to allow the soap and salt to break down the cell membranes and release the DNA.
6. Pour the mixture through a mesh strainer or gauze into a conical flask to remove the kiwi pulp and seeds.
7. Pour 5-10mL of the solution into a test.
8. Tilt the test tube at an angle. Carefully add an equal volume of ice-cold 70% ethanol down the wall of the test tube so that it sits on top of the green solution.
9. Let the mixture sit for a few minutes until the DNA becomes visible as white, stringy strands.
10. Carefully transfer the DNA strands to a new container using a toothpick or small spatula.

BACKGROUND INFORMATION: The DNA extraction method using salt and soap is a simple and effective technique for isolating DNA from a variety of organisms, including plants and fruits. The soap helps to dissolve the cell membrane and release the DNA, while the salt helps to clump the DNA together, making it easier to isolate.

title: Le Chatelier's principle
subject: Chemistry
method:
NB: Wear your safety glasses.
1. Dissolve 4 g of cobalt chloride-6-water in 40 cm3 of deionised water. The following equilibrium is set up when the crystals are added to water:
CoCl42- + 6H2O Co(H2O)62+ + 4Cl-
Blue Pink
Since the pink colour is predominant, we may conclude that the equilibrium lies
on the right hand side.
2. Using a fume cupboard, add concentrated hydrochloric acid, with stirring, until a violet solution is formed.
3. Adding more concentrated hydrochloric acid produces a blue colour, while adding water will restore the pink colour. By trial and error produce an “in between” violet (or lilac) colour which will contain the two cobalt ions. Place this solution in each of six boiling tubes to a depth of about 2 cm.
4. To study the effects of concentration changes on equilibrium, keep one tube as a control. Add water to a second tube using a dropping pipette. The colour of the solution should change to pink. The equilibrium has now shifted to the right hand side as the forward reaction absorbs the stress of the increased concentration of water.
5. Using a fume cupboard add concentrated hydrochloric acid to a third tube using a
dropping pipette. The colour of the solution should change to blue. The
equilibrium has now shifted to the left hand side since adding the concentrated
HCl increases the concentration of Cl- ions and, in keeping with Le Chatelier’s
Principle, the concentration of these ions is decreased by the backward reaction
taking place.
.
6. To study the effects of temperature changes on equilibrium, keep one tube as a control. Place another tube in a beaker of hot water (over 90 0C). Note that the colour changes to blue. This is in keeping with Le Chatelier's Principle, i.e. the endothermic reaction (reverse reaction) predominates in order to absorb the added heat.
7. Place another tube in a beaker of crushed ice and water. Note that the colour changes to pink. This is in keeping with Le Chatelier's Principle, i.e. the exothermic reaction (forward reaction) predominates in order to replace the lost heat.
(b) The equilibrium between CrO42- and Cr2O72-
NB: Wear your safety glasses.
1. Quarter fill a test tube with the solution of sodium dichromate provided. This should have an orange colour. The following equilibrium exists:
Cr2O72- + H2O 2CrO42- + 2H+
orange yellow
Since the orange colour predominates, the equilibrium must lie on the left hand
side of the equation.
2. Keep a second sample of the sodium dichromate solution in a test tube as a control.
3. Carefully add some bench dilute sodium hydroxide solution until the orange colour changes to yellow. The sodium hydroxide removes the H+ ions giving rise to a stress and therefore, in keeping with Le Chatelier's Principle, the forward reaction predominates to produce more H+ ions.
4. Carefully add dilute hydrochloric acid until the yellow colour changes back to orange. The added hydrochloric acid creates an excess of H+ ions that causes the equilibrium reaction to be shifted to the left in order to absorb this excess of H+ ions.
(c) The equilibrium between Fe3+ and Fe(CNS)2+
NB: Wear your safety glasses.
1. Mix together about 5 cm3 respectively of solutions of iron(III) chloride and potassium thiocyanate in a beaker. Note the formation of the red complex.
Fe3+ + CNS- Fe(CNS)2+
yellow red
Since the red complex above is formed, the equilibrium must lie on the right hand
side of the equation.
2. Divide the mixture into three portions in separate boiling tubes (Fig. 2). Keep one of these as a control.
3. Using a fume cupboard, add some concentrated hydrochloric acid to the second tube until the red colour disappears. In keeping with Le Chatelier's Principle, the red colour disappears as the equilibrium is shifted to the left hand side to replace the Fe3+ ions removed.
4. Add an equivalent amount of water to the third tube, and compare. This comparison should indicate that the extent of lightening of the colour is not due to a diluting effect.
5. To the second tube, add some potassium thiocyanate solution. The red complex reforms because the equilibrium is shifted to the right.

method:
Free Fall — Finding g from a v-t Graph (Topic 2.1)
1. Set up 2-3 light gates (or ticker-tape timer) at known heights along the fall path.
2. Release the object from rest and record velocity at each gate (or use tape intervals) with corresponding time.
3. Repeat 3-5 times and tabulate v against t.
4. Plot v (y-axis) against t (x-axis).
Plot & gradient: Gradient = g (acceleration due to gravity), directly from v = u + at with u = 0.
Simple Pendulum — Finding g from T² vs L (Topic 2.1/3.2)
1. Set the pendulum to a measured length L (to the centre of the bob); use small-angle swings (<10 degrees).
2. Time 10 full oscillations; repeat twice more and average.
3. Calculate period T = average time
10, then T-squared.
4. Repeat for at least 6 different lengths L; plot T-squared (y-axis) against L (x-axis).
Plot & gradient: Gradient = 4π²/g, from T² = (4π²/g)L — rearrange to extract g.
Newton's Second Law — Finding Mass from a vs F (Topic 2.2)
1. Level the track and confirm it is friction-compensated (trolley moves at constant velocity when given a gentle push).
2. Attach string over the pulley to a hanging mass; keep total mass (trolley + hanger + masses) constant by moving mass between trolley and hanger between runs.
3. For each hanging mass, record acceleration a via light gates; calculate applied force F = mg.
4. Plot a (y-axis) against F (x-axis).
Plot & gradient: Gradient = 1/M (inverse of total accelerated mass), from F = Ma — invert the gradient to find M.
Hooke's Law — Finding Spring Constant from F vs Extension (Topic 2.2)
1. Hang the spring vertically and record its natural (unstretched) length.
2. Add masses incrementally; record total length each time.
3. Calculate extension x = new length - natural length, and applied force F = mg, for each mass added.
4. Plot F (y-axis) against x (x-axis).
Plot & gradient: Gradient = k (spring constant), directly from F = kx. Note where the graph stops being linear (elastic limit).
Energy Conservation on a Ramp — Finding g from v² vs h (Topic 2.3/3.1)
1. Set the ramp at a starting height h (measured vertically, not along the slope) and mark a fixed release point.
2. Release the trolley from rest; record its velocity at the bottom of the ramp using the light gate.
3. Repeat for at least 6 different heights h; square each velocity to get v-squared.
4. Plot v-squared (y-axis) against h (x-axis).
Plot & gradient: Gradient = 2g, from mgh = ½mv² → v² = 2gh — halve the gradient to find g.

title: Chlorophyll chromatography
subject: Biology

kit.name: Watman® no.1 chromatography paper (Long strip longer than boiling tube)
Bung for boiling tube (Or aluminum foil to cover container)
Small amount of sand (For grinding. I table spoon should be enough)

method:
You are using propanone, which is a highly flammable and irritant chemical. You must make sure there are no naked flames in the room at any time. You should try not to breathe too many fumes and keep containers with propanone covered. Safety glasses must be worn when preparing the slide.
1. Cut up some leaves into small pieces.
2. Put the leaf pieces into a mortar to about 2 cm depth.
3. Add about six drops of propanone using a Pasteur pipette.
4. Grind the mixture with a pestle for at least 3 minutes. If the leaves are very thick, add a small quantity of sand to help the cells to break.
5. Cut a strip of chromatography paper to fit into a large test-tube or small beaker.
6. Draw a pencil line 15 mm from one end of the chromatography paper.
7. Using a pencil, mark places on this line where the leaf extract will be placed. This is the origin.
8. Use a capillary tube to draw up liquid from around the crushed leaves.
9. Touch the capillary on to the origin mark on the chromatography paper. The leaf extract will flow onto the paper. You must keep the spot as small as possible (no more than 2 mm).
10. Allow the spot to dry and then add another spot on top.
11. Add 5 more spots of solution, letting each one dry before putting on the next. This should give a very concentrated small spot on the paper.
12. Put propanone into a large test-tube or small beaker until there is a 10 mm depth.
13. If you are using a large test-tube:
place it into a rack or other support. Lower the chromatography paper into the test- tube with the origin towards the propanone. The end of the paper should just touch the propanone. Do not allow it to rise above the origin. Fold the other end of the paper over the edge of the test-tube and insert a stopper. Try not to move the test- tube. If you are using a beaker:
fold the top end of the paper over a pencil and lower the paper into the beaker with the origin towards the propanone. The end of the paper should just touch the propanone. Do not allow it to rise above the origin. Cover the beaker with metal foil or parafilm. Try not to move the beaker.
14. Leave the apparatus to allow the propanone to rise up the paper and separate the pigments in the leaf extract. This is called ‘running a chromatogram’.
15. Observe the order in which the different colours of pigment appear.
16. When the propanone is about 10 mm from the top of the paper, remove the paper and mark the position of the solvent. This is the solvent front.
17. Leave the chromatogram to dry.
18. The crushed leaves and the used propanone must be disposed of safely.

title: DNA electrophoresis
subject: Biology

kit.name: Bunsen burner, tripod and gauze or access to a microwave

method:
Preparing and pouring the agarose
1. Add 0.35 g of agarose powder to 35 cm3 of TBE buffer in a conical flask.
2. Heat the mixture over a Bunsen burner using a tripod and gauze, swirling the flask occasionally to prevent any lumps forming. If a microwave is available, heat for 30 seconds, then in units of 10 seconds until the agarose dissolves.
3. Agarose becomes transparent when it boils. When it reaches this stage, remove from the heat and leave to cool for 6-8 minutes or until the temperature of the agarose is between 55 °C and 60 °C.
4. Whilst the gel is cooling, prepare the electrophoresis tank by inserting the casting gates and comb.
5. When the gel has cooled sufficiently to the desired temperature it can be carefully poured into the tank, between the two casting gates.
6. Leave the gel to set for at least 15 minutes. Loading the gel
7. Once the gel is set, carefully remove the casting gates.
8. Very gently remove the comb, taking care not to rip the gel. The comb should have introduced ‘wells’ into the gel for loading the dyes.
9. Pour 40 cm3 TBE buffer into the tank. This should completely cover the surface of the gel.
10. Fill a micropipette or capillary tube with dye A.
11. Position the pipette or capillary inside the mouth of the first well in the gel and dispense the dye into it.
12. Load dye B into the next well in the same way.
13. Repeat the loading procedure for each of the dyes available.
14. Connect the battery pack. The negative electrode should be at the same end as the wells loaded with dye.
15. After a minimum of 1.5 hours and a maximum of 3 hours, disconnect the battery pack and record the results.
prepNotes:
Once prepared, agarose gel has a short shelf life and should be discarded after removal from the electrophoresis tank.
TBE buffer is effective to a minimum of a 10% working concentration and has a shelf life of approximately 12 months.
Possible variables to control include: temperature, pH, concentration of TBE buffer, volume of TBE buffer, electrical charge through the gel.
It is convenient to make more of the reagents than is required in order to give sufficient quantities for accurate measurements.
Very small quantities of dye solutions are needed. 1 cm 3 is sufficient for 3 or 4 learners. These can be provided in a number of ways, either separately or in various mixtures. Other dyes that might be used are bromophenol blue and bromocresol green. Alternatively, red food colouring, blue food colouring, green food colouring, yellow food colouring can be used. The dye samples should be provided in small specimen tubes, labelled A, B, C, D, etc.
It is expected that an electrophoresis kit will be available. Each kit usually has its own individual way of connecting a battery pack but will include instructions. For a practical that incorporates more aspects of DNA fingerprinting, including cutting DNA with restriction enzymes for example, the purchase of a kit that includes all the necessary materials is advised. A number of companies produce kits with instructions for practical activities.
If electrophoresis kits are not available, they can be made using plastic boxes as buffer tanks, glass sheets for supporting a gel, a pair of electrodes (platinum is preferred although carbon will work) and a 9 V battery. A thin plastic sheet can be cut to form a comb. title: Membrane permeability (beetroot)
subject: Biology
method:
Preparation of washed beetroot cylinders
First prepare 10 cylinders of beetroot.
Cut them out of the beetroot with a "cork borer".
Wash them in a beaker of cold water.
Use a scalpel to make them all the same length.
Aim for 2cm length, but you might have to use shorter pieces.
The key thing is that they are all the same length.
Prepare 10 diffusion solutions – where the beetroot will rest after heating
Set up 10 test tubes into 2 test tube racks.
Put 5cm3 of distilled water into each test tube.
Put each rack onto a piece of A4 paper for noting stopwatch times later.
Label the tubes in the rack with the temperature of the Heat Treatment the beetroot will have received before diffusion. “70°C”, “65°C”, “60°C”, etc. to 25°C. Note: these solutions will be at room temperature.
Use water from the electronic water bath to make a "beaker water bath" using 150ml of hot water at 80°C in a 250ml beaker. Put a thermometer in it too.
Heat Treatment
This procedure requires good preparation as the temperature cools quickly at the beginning.
1. Set up a clean electronic water bath at 80°C.
2. Use water from the electronic water bath to make a "beaker water bath" using 150ml of hot water at 80°C in a 250ml beaker. Put a thermometer in it too.
3. When the water has cooled to 70°C put in the first beetroot cylinder, for exactly 60 seconds. Leave the stopwatch running for the whole experiment.
4. Take out the beetroot and put it into the diffusion solution labelled 70°C for 15 minutes. (Note the time on the stopwatch on the A4 paper – you will leave it for 15 minutes).
5. When your water bath has cooled to 65°C put in the next beetroot cylinder, for 60 seconds.
6. Put this beetroot cylinder into the diffusion solution labelled 70°C for 15 minutes.
7. Repeat steps 5 & 6 again at 60°C, 55°C, 50°C and so on to 25°C.
8. Ensure that all the beetroot samples have exactly
a) 60 seconds heat treatment and
b) 15 minutes diffusion time to make this a fair test.
9. Take each piece of beetroot out of the diffusion solutions after exactly 15 minutes.
10. Save the labelled diffusion solutions for the colorimeter.
11. Record notes for you qualitative observations.
Colorimeter Readings
When more pigment has diffused out of the beetroot cells the diffusion solution will be a darker purple colour. We can measure the colour intensity using a colorimeter.
1. Two thirds fill the plastic colorimeter cuvette with the diffusion solution.
2. Put the cuvette into the colorimeter slot. Check the mark on the cuvette is at the front. (The machine needs careful calibration first to get good results)
3. Note down the reading which you get.
4. Check that you are measuring the amount of light absorbed by the beetroot pigment. (measuring the amount of light passing through your solution, % Transmission) 5. Repeat with all the other solutions and record your results in a table of your own. 6. Note the uncertainty, i.e. the precision of your colorimeter.

method:
1. Cut off 1-2 cm of the root tips. Put in a small volume of ethanoic acid on a watch glass for 10 minutes.
2. After 10 minutes, rinse the roots thoroughly in tap water.
3. Cover the roots in HCl and place the watch glass on a hot plate (55ºC - 60ºC) for 5 minutes.
4. Rinse the roots and dry them on a paper towel.

7. Use the mounted needle to remove root tips onto a clean microscope slide.
